02 | South 01.title: Nursery on Schenkweg
02 | South 01.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | South 01.medium: Black chalk, graphite, pen, brush, and ink, heightened with white body color on laid paper watermarked ED & CIE (in a cartouche)
02 | South 01.body:
A nursery near Vincent’s studio became the subject of this drawing. It belonged to a group of views of The Hague commissioned by his uncle, the art dealer C. M. van Gogh. For the young artist, the work offered an opportunity to earn money through drawing.

Before sending it away, Vincent revised the foreground following advice from his friend Anthon van Rappard. He looked more closely at the ditch and the water. He felt that these changes helped the scene express spring and a gentle stillness.

Payment arrived in early June, without a letter. Vincent was left wondering whether his uncle liked the drawings and whether more work would follow.
02 | South 01.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 1972.118.281

02 | South 02.title: Gardener by an Apple Tree
02 | South 02.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | South 02.medium: Transfer lithograph with pen and ink
02 | South 02.body:
A gardener bends into his work beneath an apple tree. The image grew from an encounter Van Gogh described to Theo in July 1883. After watching a gardener at a home for elderly people, he developed the figure with the help of a familiar model.

Making the print brought another set of difficulties. Fine lines had to survive transfer and printing, and this particular impression was extensively strengthened by hand. The dark marks around the tree preserve some of that continued work.

Here, an ordinary working body becomes the centre of an experiment involving memory, a sitter, printing materials, and revision.
02 | South 02.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 2021.241

02 | South 03.title: Avenue of Pollard Birches and Poplars
02 | South 03.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | South 03.medium: Reed pen and iron-gall ink on tan laid paper
02 | South 03.body:
Follow the rows of trees towards the small figure on the road. Repeated trunks and closely worked lines carry the eye into the distance.

Van Gogh made this drawing in Nuenen in March 1884. Around this time, he was reading François Coppée, a poet whose attention to ordinary lives interested him. The Art Institute of Chicago suggests a connection with Coppée’s poem Tristement.

The drawing has also changed materially. Its iron-gall ink has become brown, and some neighbouring lines have blurred together. The sheet we encounter today carries the effects of both Van Gogh’s drawing and the materials’ ageing.
02 | South 03.credit: The Art Institute of Chicago · Public-domain image via Wikimedia Commons · 2022.74

02 | South 04.title: A Peasant Woman Digging in Front of Her Cottage
02 | South 04.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | South 04.body:
A woman bends towards the soil close to a cottage. Her work, the surrounding ground, and the building share a closely related range of earthy colours.

In Nuenen, Van Gogh walked through the countryside looking for cottages and people at work. His letters reveal an affection for small dwellings, which he sometimes associated with birds’ nests. That image helps us approach the closeness of shelter and daily labour here.

The woman’s identity is unknown. Her posture remains visible: a body directing its weight into a familiar task, within a landscape Van Gogh was learning to paint.
02 | South 04.credit: The Art Institute of Chicago · Public-domain image via Wikimedia Commons · 1968.92

02 | South 05.title: The Potato Peeler
02 | South 05.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | South 05.body:
A woman prepares potatoes, absorbed in the work of her hands. Van Gogh painted this study in Nuenen in early 1885, during a period of sustained attention to rural people and their daily activities. The restricted palette and firm, block-like forms belong to that developing practice.

The same canvas continued to serve him. In Paris in 1887, he painted a self-portrait on its other side.

Turning between the two images brings two moments of his working life into contact. The cloth carries a rural figure study and a later experiment in painting his own face.
02 | South 05.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 67.187.70b

02 | South 06.title: Potato Eaters (lithograph)
02 | South 06.body:
Before completing the final oil painting of The Potato Eaters, Van Gogh made a lithograph of the subject. In April 1885, he arranged printing in Eindhoven and sent impressions to Theo, hoping the image would reach people who might take an interest in his work.

The print carries a reversed composition and a reversed signature. It preserves an earlier stage in the subject’s development, along with the practical consequences of printing.

One impression also became part of a difficult exchange with his friend Anthon van Rappard. Making the image public brought responses that Van Gogh could not control.
02 | South 06.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington · Open Access / CC0 · 1951.10.33 · National Gallery of Art, Washington · F1661 / JH737 / 1951.10.33
02 | South 06.provenanceNote: The F/JH number identifies the print design. This image is the National Gallery of Art impression, accession 1951.10.33, not the Amsterdam impression illustrated in the letter edition.
02 | South 06.medium: Crayon lithograph with scraping, printed in dark brown on thin wove paper

01 | Fan 01 | painting.title: Road in Etten
01 | Fan 01 | painting.creator: Vincent van Gogh
01 | Fan 01 | painting.medium: Chalk, pencil, pastel and watercolour; underdrawing in pen and brown ink
01 | Fan 01 | painting.body:
A man sweeps a road lined with pollard willows. The trees and the narrowing path draw the eye into the distance, while the small working figure gives the landscape a human presence. Vincent made this drawing during his stay in Etten in 1881, when local workers and their everyday tasks became recurring subjects.

Soon after returning, he told Theo how pleased he was to have time to work quietly. He hoped to make many studies and asked his brother to keep him informed about opportunities for a draughtsman. His future was taking shape through repeated practice.

Months later, he wrote enthusiastically to his friend Anthon van Rappard about the old willows along a local road. He wanted his friend to come and see them too.
01 | Fan 01 | painting.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 459193

03 | South 01.title: Le Moulin de la Galette
03 | South 01.body:
In Paris, Van Gogh found subjects close to the apartment he shared with Theo. Montmartre’s streets and windmills gave him places to return to with his painting materials.

This view of the Moulin de la Galette records a quiet corner of that neighbourhood. The colours remain restrained, while passages of red, green, blue, and orange reveal his growing interest in how colours act upon one another.

His Paris work developed through individual pictures like this one. A familiar street became a place to test decisions about light, brushwork, and the organisation of a painted surface.
03 | South 01.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; see source page for version and collection · Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin · F228 / JH1171
03 | South 01.institution: Alte Nationalgalerie, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
03 | South 01.provenanceNote: Identity follows the scholarly Van Gogh Letters edition. Collection names are documented source attributions, not independently verified current ownership.

03 | South 02.title: Self-Portrait with a Straw Hat
03 | South 02.creator: Vincent van Gogh
03 | South 02.body:
A straw hat frames Van Gogh’s face, while short strokes of colour build the head, clothing, and background. During his Paris years, he repeatedly painted himself as he developed his skills in figure painting.

Money helped shape that practice. His own face was available to study in a mirror, and this portrait was painted on the other side of an earlier peasant study.

The canvas brings artistic experiment close to the practical life of the studio. A mirror, an existing support, and repeated sessions of looking gave him material for another picture.
03 | South 02.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436532

03 | South 03.title: Sunflowers (Paris)
03 | South 03.creator: Vincent van Gogh
03 | South 03.body:
Two cut sunflower heads fill the foreground. Their petals curl around dense centres, offering Vincent a subject rich in texture, shape, and colour.

He painted four sunflower still lifes in Paris in late summer 1887. This canvas belongs to that period of repeated looking and experiment. Close to the flowers, individual marks become visible; at a distance, they gather into the weight and structure of the heads.

These paintings also entered the lives of other artists. Gauguin acquired two smaller works from the Paris group and displayed them in his apartment. An everyday studio subject became part of an artistic relationship.
03 | South 03.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436524

03 | South 04.title: Père Tanguy
03 | South 04.body:
Julien-François Tanguy sold the materials that made paintings possible. At his small shop on the Rue Clauzel, artists could sometimes exchange their work for supplies. Vincent painted him three times.

Here, Tanguy sits facing us, his hands resting together. Around him, Japanese prints fill the background with colour and images of distant places. The portrait brings a familiar Parisian shopkeeper into the visual world Vincent was studying.

Their relationship belonged to everyday life, with purchases, assistance, disagreements, and renewed contact. Looking at this painting, we meet someone whose practical support helped sustain an artist’s work.
03 | South 04.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; see source page for version and collection · Paris, Musée Rodin · F363 / JH1351
03 | South 04.provenanceNote: Identity follows the scholarly Van Gogh Letters edition. Collection names are documented source attributions, not independently verified current ownership.

03 | South 05.title: Bridge in the Rain (after Hiroshige)
03 | South 05.creator: Vincent van Gogh
03 | South 05.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
03 | South 05.body:
A bridge crosses the picture as people move through a sudden shower. Vincent encountered this scene in a Japanese woodcut by Utagawa Hiroshige.

In Paris, he translated the printed image into oil paint. He intensified its colours and retained the proportions of the source within a larger canvas. The surrounding border gave him additional space, which he filled with characters copied from other Japanese prints.

This painting lets us follow a particular act of learning. Vincent studied an image made in another place and medium, then worked through its structure with his own materials. Hiroshige’s design remains essential to that encounter.

03 | North 01.title: Flowering Plum Orchard (after Hiroshige)
03 | North 01.creator: Vincent van Gogh
03 | North 01.body:
A large trunk crosses the foreground. Beyond it, small figures move among flowering trees. Vincent encountered this garden through a colour woodcut by Utagawa Hiroshige, an artist working in Edo.

In Paris, Japanese prints became part of Vincent and Theo’s collection. Vincent studied their compositions closely. A surviving tracing of this image brings us near that work, following the branches and the arrangement of the garden.

His painted version preserves Hiroshige’s design while introducing stronger colours. Red and blue enter the trunk. Orange borders widen the image, carrying characters borrowed from another print.

This painting gives us a concrete view of an artist learning. He follows an existing image, studies its structure and tests what happens when it takes shape in oil paint.
03 | North 01.labelTitle: A Tree He Learned to See Through

04 | Fan 01 | painting.title: The Flowering Orchard
04 | Fan 01 | painting.creator: Vincent van Gogh
04 | Fan 01 | painting.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
04 | Fan 01 | painting.body:
Branches spread across a pale sky. Blossom gathers along them, while a scythe and rake rest in the grass below.

During his first spring in Arles, Vincent worked repeatedly among flowering fruit trees. The season gave him a subject with a short working life. Around 20 April 1888, he told Theo that most of the orchards had already lost their blossom and that he would have to change subjects.

This painting belongs to that sustained attention to the trees. The Metropolitan Museum of Art connects its angular branches with Vincent’s admiration for Japanese prints.

His letters also preserve the difficulties of the work. He counted canvases, considered how they might form a decoration and judged some results harshly. The flowering orchard brings us close to both his ambition and the practical limits of a passing season.
04 | Fan 01 | painting.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436527
04 | Fan 01 | painting.collectionCredit: The Mr. and Mrs. Henry Ittleson Jr. Purchase Fund, 1956
04 | Fan 01 | painting.labelTitle: Working While the Trees Were in Blossom

04 | Fan 02 | painting.title: Oleanders
04 | Fan 02 | painting.creator: Vincent van Gogh
04 | Fan 02 | painting.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
04 | Fan 02 | painting.body:
Pink flowers and pointed leaves spread from a ceramic jug. Beside it lies a yellow-covered book, identified as Émile Zola’s La joie de vivre.

Around 13 August 1888, Vincent told Theo that he hoped to paint a study of oleanders in the coming days. Later that month, he mentioned a bouquet in progress. The published correspondence leaves its precise identification open.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art reads the flowers as life-affirming and connects them symbolically with the novel. The jug also belongs to Vincent’s practical world: he used it in other still lifes in Arles.

These objects bring several parts of his life onto one table. Flowers supplied a subject, a familiar vessel held them, and a book brought reading into the painted arrangement. His letters from the same weeks keep the surrounding work visible through models, rent and requests for money.
04 | Fan 02 | painting.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436530
04 | Fan 02 | painting.collectionCredit: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Loeb, 1962
04 | Fan 02 | painting.labelTitle: Flowers, a Book and a Working Life

04 | Fan 03 | painting.title: The Yellow House (The Street)
04 | Fan 03 | painting.creator: Vincent van Gogh
04 | Fan 03 | painting.body:
In September 1888, Vincent was preparing a home in Arles. He had rented four rooms in the yellow corner building several months earlier. Now he was buying beds, chairs and linen, arranging a studio downstairs and making room for a guest upstairs. He imagined paintings covering the walls and friends sharing the space.

This view brings his daily surroundings together. The restaurant where he ate appears on the left. Railway bridges stand farther along the street. His rooms are marked by green shutters. In a letter to Theo, he described the challenge of painting the yellow buildings and ground beneath a cobalt-blue sky.

A place to stay was becoming part of his working life. Each purchase required money, each room suggested possibilities, and the arrival of a fellow painter remained something to prepare for.
04 | Fan 03 | painting.labelTitle: A Place to Live and Work

04 | Fan 04 | painting.title: Terrace of a Café at Night (Place du Forum)
04 | Fan 04 | painting.creator: Vincent van Gogh
04 | Fan 04 | painting.commonsFile: File:Van Gogh - Terrasse des Cafés an der Place du Forum in Arles am Abend1.jpeg
04 | Fan 04 | painting.body:
A gas lamp lights the café terrace and sends colour across the pavement. Beyond its reach, the street recedes through blue and violet towards a sky scattered with stars. Small figures sit at tables or move through the square.

Vincent painted this scene in Arles in September 1888. Writing to his sister Wil, he described a night picture made with blue, violet and green, without black. He enjoyed working outdoors after dark, although the conditions made colours difficult to distinguish.

He also connected the subject with his reading. The illuminated cafés and starry Parisian evening at the beginning of Maupassant’s Bel-Ami reminded him of the scene he had painted. Observation and literature met in an ordinary public place.

04 | Fan 05 | painting.title: Le café de nuit (The Night Café)
04 | Fan 05 | painting.body:
Vincent stayed awake for three nights to paint this room, sleeping during the day. In September 1888, he described the work to Theo through red walls, yellow lamps, a green billiard table and small figures seated beneath the high ceiling.

He wanted colour to carry emotion. His letters connect the reds and greens with disturbing human passions and the atmosphere of a place where a person might lose their bearings. He had also described night cafés as shelters for people unable to afford lodging or too drunk to be admitted elsewhere.

He judged the painting harshly, calling it one of his ugliest works, while explaining its purpose with care. The letters reveal a sustained attempt to make an unsettling public room speak through colour.
04 | Fan 05 | painting.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain · New Haven, Yale University Art Gallery, Bequest of Stephen Carlton Clark, B.A. 1903 · F463 / JH1575
04 | Fan 05 | painting.institution: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven
04 | Fan 05 | painting.provenanceNote: Object metadata and collection credit follow the Yale University Art Gallery record. The installed image retains its separate Wikimedia Commons public-domain record.
04 | Fan 05 | painting.collectionCredit: Bequest of Stephen Carlton Clark, B.A. 1903

04 | South 01.title: Madame Roulin and Her Baby
04 | South 01.body:
Augustine Roulin holds her daughter Marcelle close to her body. Vincent painted members of the Roulin household during his time in Arles, returning to the people around his friend Joseph Roulin. In this picture, the baby's face receives particularly concentrated attention, while Augustine's features are indicated more briefly.

Look at the space between the two faces and the movement of the supporting arm. The subject brings the exhibition into the everyday work of holding and caring for a child.

We can identify these sitters and place the painting within the family portrait group. Their exact experience of this sitting, and every feeling Vincent brought to it, remain beyond the surviving evidence.
04 | South 01.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 459123
04 | South 01.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

04 | South 02.title: Street in Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer
04 | South 02.creator: Vincent van Gogh
04 | South 02.medium: Reed pen, quill and brown ink over graphite on wove paper
04 | South 02.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
04 | South 02.body:
Thatched roofs, smoking chimneys and a road through the village fill this drawing. Vincent had encountered the subject during his visit to Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer in early June 1888, when he painted a view of the street.

The sheet shown here came later. In July, he returned to the painted composition and created it again in pen and ink. It became one of fifteen drawings sent that month to Émile Bernard in Brittany.

The change of medium required a new set of decisions. Roofs, walls and the road are described through strokes, dots and areas of dense ink. A painted scene becomes something a friend can examine on paper.

This drawing records an exchange between artists at a distance. Vincent used it to share what he was working on and to keep a conversation moving.
04 | South 02.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 336318
04 | South 02.labelTitle: A Street Sent to a Friend

05 | South 01.title: Van Gogh's Chair
05 | South 01.body:
A rush-seated chair holds a pipe and tobacco. Behind it, a wooden box contains sprouting bulbs. Vincent gave ordinary things a place within a paired project: this chair and the chair he painted for Gauguin. The National Gallery understands the pair as portraits conveyed through furnishings and personal objects.

The picture also carries a history of revision. On 17 January 1889, Vincent told Theo that he had worked on his chair painting again that day.

For the exhibition, the paired images give the shared house a human scale. Start with its furniture, the objects left on a seat, and the different ways two people could be represented within the same home.

05 | South 02.title: Gauguin's Chair
05 | South 02.body:
A candle burns on the seat of an armchair beside two books. Another light hangs on the wall. The room has an occupant through the objects placed there, even though no figure appears.

Vincent painted this chair as a companion to his own. The Van Gogh Museum interprets the pair as portraits of the two artists through their furniture and belongings.

Their shared life in Arles also involved continued work on pictures. In January 1889, Vincent was still writing about the chair paintings and revisions.

Look at this interior at the scale of a room someone used. The curved wood, the bright seat and the surrounding shadows offer a way of approaching an individual through a place. Later events belong in the historical record; the chair can first be encountered through its painted details.
05 | South 02.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

05 | South 03.title: The Lullaby (Augustine Roulin)
05 | South 03.body:
Augustine Roulin holds the cord of a cradle outside the frame. The portrait combines her seated presence with an action we complete in our imagination. This canvas is one of five versions of the subject. According to the Met, it is the version Augustine chose for herself.

That choice gives the story another voice, even though we do not have her own account of it. She had an opportunity to judge the pictures and select one.

Vincent later discussed versions as possible gifts to other artists.  Their circulation could involve sitters, friends and recipients, each with a different relationship to the image. In this exhibition, Augustine's choice keeps our attention on the person whose likeness became the series' centre.
05 | South 03.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 437984
05 | South 03.catalogueTitle: La Berceuse (Woman Rocking a Cradle; Augustine-Alix Pellicot Roulin, 1851–1930)
05 | South 03.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
05 | South 03.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1996, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002

05 | South 04.title: The Woman from Arles (Madame Ginoux)
05 | South 04.body: A portrait of the café owner, in the version held by The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
05 | South 04.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436529

05 | South 05.title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
05 | South 05.body:
Vincent painted this portrait shortly after returning from hospital in January 1889. The bandage records a serious injury. Around him are the materials and images of a painter's room: a canvas on an easel and a Japanese print. The Courtauld interprets their presence, together with the assured handling of paint, as a statement of renewed work.

His letter of 17 January gives that return a practical setting. It includes pictures completed, money owed and expenses connected with treatment and painting.

The exhibition allows those activities to remain together. A person receiving care was also making pictures, buying materials and trying to report his circumstances to his brother.
05 | South 05.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; see source page for version details
05 | South 05.institution: The Courtauld Gallery, London (Samuel Courtauld Trust)

06 | Curved wall -1 0.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses
06 | Curved wall -1 0.body:
In June 1889, Vincent painted this landscape outdoors near Saint-Rémy. Wheat, shrubs, cypresses, hills and clouds occupy successive parts of the canvas. He returned to the composition in later versions, carrying an observed subject into further work.

On 2 July, he described the sky through a comparison with a multicoloured Scottish plaid. The comparison gives us access to a painter thinking about interwoven colours and shapes.

Follow those shapes across the surface. The clouds gather in rounded strokes; the field is worked in shorter marks; the cypresses rise at the right. This exhibition places the picture within the practical activity of going out, observing and returning to a composition.
06 | Curved wall -1 0.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436535
06 | Curved wall -1 0.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

06 | Curved wall -1 1.title: Olive Trees
06 | Curved wall -1 1.body:
The trunks turn through a field of broken colour. Short strokes travel across the ground, then collect into the trees' foliage. The orchard offers a place to look repeatedly, with shifting light and different relationships between earth, leaves and sky.

In November 1889, Vincent was discussing the religious pictures of Gauguin and Bernard. He responded critically and described his own work among olive trees in clear, cold weather. His letters place the grove within a continuing conversation about how pictures should be made.

The Met identifies this canvas with that November campaign.  Here, a walk into an orchard becomes part of a working argument: attend to a place, test what you see, and develop a painted response through repeated attempts.
06 | Curved wall -1 1.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 437998
06 | Curved wall -1 1.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
06 | Curved wall -1 1.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1998, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002

06 | Curved wall -1 2.title: Irises (in a vase)
06 | Curved wall -1 2.body:
In May 1890, Vincent painted four ambitious bouquets before leaving Saint-Rémy. This vase of irises belonged to that group.

The flowers have been gathered into an interior arrangement. Leaves and petals spread across the wide canvas, held together by the vase and the limited space around it. The image gives us another way to follow a subject he had already studied in the garden.

In a June letter to Willemien, Vincent recalled the flower paintings and their intended colour relationships.  The colours we see today have also changed through the fading of red pigments.

Here, a familiar subject marks a new working situation. The flowers were cut, arranged and painted close to the end of his stay. Their presence provides a concrete point of entry into those days.
06 | Curved wall -1 2.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436528
06 | Curved wall -1 2.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

06 | Curved wall -1 3.title: Cypresses
06 | Curved wall -1 3.body:
The trees occupy almost the full height of the canvas. Small changes in the direction of the strokes make their dark forms feel dense and restless. The sky remains visible around them, while the lower vegetation brings the eye back towards the ground.

In June 1889, Vincent wrote about his wish to paint cypresses. Their proportions reminded him of an obelisk, and their dark green presented a particular challenge against the surrounding light.

This painting belongs to his close study of a subject he continued to develop. It later appeared at the Salon des Indépendants in 1890.

Begin with the difficulty he described: how can a very dark tree remain distinct, varied and alive within a bright landscape? The question connects his written ambitions with the physical marks on the canvas.
06 | Curved wall -1 3.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 437980
06 | Curved wall -1 3.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

06 | Curved wall -1 4.title: First Steps, after Millet
06 | Curved wall -1 4.body:
A child moves between two adults. Arms reach across the small space, and the surrounding garden gives the action an everyday setting.

Vincent worked from a photograph of Millet's composition sent by Theo. He used a grid to transfer its structure onto canvas, then developed the colour.

In correspondence, he compared interpreting another artist's work with performing music. A composition could be received, studied and given an individual rendering.

This painting therefore carries several kinds of contact: with an admired predecessor, with the brother who supplied the image, and with a subject of care and tentative movement. The family's action belongs to Millet's source. Vincent's work gives us a way to follow how that image was made newly present through another painter's materials and decisions.
06 | Curved wall -1 4.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436526
06 | Curved wall -1 4.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
06 | Curved wall -1 4.collectionCredit: Gift of George N. and Helen M. Richard, 1964

06 | Curved wall 1 0.title: Corridor in the Asylum
06 | Curved wall 1 0.body:
A corridor extends through the image. Repeated openings and arches carry the eye inward, while changes in light make sections of the passage distinct.

Vincent made this work on paper in September 1889 and sent it to Theo to show his surroundings at Saint-Rémy.  It belongs to an exchange between brothers as well as to the record of a building.

The materials are specific: black chalk under drawing, brush-applied oils and pink laid paper.  Look closely at the relationship between drawn structure and painted surface.

For this exhibition, the passage gives the story a place to inhabit. Its architecture can feel enclosing, distant or quiet to different viewers. Those impressions remain responses to an image, held alongside what the object record can tell us about its making and purpose.
06 | Curved wall 1 0.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 336327
06 | Curved wall 1 0.medium: Brush and oils over black chalk on pink laid paper
06 | Curved wall 1 0.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

06 | Curved wall 1 1.title: Women Picking Olives
06 | Curved wall 1 1.body:
Figures work beneath the olive trees. Their gestures bring a repeated human activity into the orchard, joining the bent trunks and the ground's patterned surface.

Vincent developed this subject in three versions. The Met identifies its canvas as the most resolved of the group and records that he intended it for his mother and sister.

That intended destination gives the scene a relationship beyond the place it depicts. A picture of southern work could become something to share with family elsewhere. In this exhibition, we can follow that connection without inventing the recipients' response.

Look at the small intervals between bodies, branches and earth. The story unfolds through ordinary movement: reach, bend, gather, and begin again. These are looking prompts offered by the exhibition, grounded in the figures visible before us.
06 | Curved wall 1 1.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 436536
06 | Curved wall 1 1.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
06 | Curved wall 1 1.collectionCredit: The Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg Collection, Gift of Walter H. and Leonore Annenberg, 1995, Bequest of Walter H. Annenberg, 2002

06 | Curved wall 1 2.title: The Starry Night
06 | Curved wall 1 2.body:
Vincent wrote about looking out before sunrise and seeing a large morning star. A later June letter mentions a new study of a starry sky.  These are traces of looking and working, attached to particular moments in his correspondence.

On the canvas, the sky fills most of the space. A cypress rises close to the viewer, and a village gathers below the hills. MoMA explains the scene through a combination of observation, memory and imagination; the village is constructed, with a church spire recalling Dutch architecture.

The picture allows the distant and the remembered to occupy one place. We can approach its making through the painter's choices while remaining careful about what the image can tell us about his health. A painted sky is not a clinical record.
06 | Curved wall 1 2.institution: The Museum of Modern Art, New York
06 | Curved wall 1 2.collectionCredit: Acquired through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest

07 | Horizon -1 0.title: Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe
07 | Horizon -1 0.body:
The face at the centre of this small print belongs to the world of Auvers. Its title leaves room for two descriptions: Doctor Gachet, or a man with a pipe. The print holds a likeness together with the practical question of how an image can be made and circulated.

The Metropolitan Museum identifies Paul-Ferdinand Gachet as the printer. The folded sheet also preserves an inscription connected with an artist's proof. Vincent was therefore involved in more than the act of drawing. The image passed through a working relationship that included a sitter, a plate, an impression and a person with access to a press.

On 17 June 1890, Vincent wrote to Theo about the possibility of making several more etchings of southern subjects, with Gachet printing them. He imagined a small group of works and mentioned the possibility of Gauguin's participation. The proposal remained incomplete.

This object asks us to look at reproduction as part of artistic practice. One etched composition can survive in several impressions. Each impression has its own paper, inscriptions, condition and history. The exhibition keeps those levels separate while following the plan that briefly connected portraiture, friendship and printmaking.
07 | Horizon -1 0.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Open Access / CC0 · 849056
07 | Horizon -1 0.catalogueTitle: Portrait of Doctor Gachet or Man with a Pipe
07 | Horizon -1 0.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

07 | Horizon -1 1.title: The Church at Auvers
07 | Horizon -1 1.body:
The church rises from a low viewpoint, its walls divided into strong colour and its roof gathered beneath a blue sky. The composition looks towards the rear of the building. The missing front entrance belongs to the chosen view. It does not provide a complete explanation of Vincent's relationship to religion.

On 5 June 1890, Vincent described the painting to Willemien. He mentioned cobalt, violet and orange, and connected the Auvers church with the old church tower at Nuenen.  The letter brings an earlier landscape into the later one. A building in Auvers becomes part of a personal history of places, memories and repeated subjects.

The church is familiar enough to recognise and unfamiliar enough to remain unsettled. Its curved lines do not settle into a single architectural rhythm. The surrounding paths and grass hold the building in place while the colour keeps the surface active.

This work belongs to the documented life of Auvers. Its meaning can be approached through colour, viewpoint, correspondence and earlier memory. It should not be reduced to a diagnosis or to a single story about belief.

07 | Horizon -1 2.title: Daubigny's Garden
07 | Horizon -1 2.body: One version of a garden Vincent painted several times at Auvers.

07 | Horizon -1 3.title: Wheatfield under Thunderclouds
07 | Horizon -1 3.body:
The field stretches across the canvas in a long horizontal band. Above it, clouds gather and open across a dark sky. The landscape offers very little shelter. Its scale gives the viewer room to move through the image, while its compressed height keeps the ground close to the horizon.

The Van Gogh Museum places the painting among the wheatfields Vincent completed around Auvers in the last weeks of his life. In a letter to Theo and Jo, he described sadness and extreme loneliness, then also wrote about what he considered healthy and fortifying in the countryside.  These words belong to the same late period. They do not function as a private caption written for this canvas.

The unusual elongated format emphasises the breadth of the scene. Two broad horizontal zones carry most of the composition: earth below and sky above. The painting holds weather and human language in the same space. It allows us to read the landscape through a documented letter while continuing to look at what the paint itself does.

The work remains a landscape before it becomes a symbol. Its clouds can be studied as forms, its field as a surface, and its scale as a decision made during the final weeks at Auvers.
07 | Horizon -1 3.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
07 | Horizon -1 3.storyGroup: A Landscape Held Between Weather and Words

07 | Horizon -1 4.title: Wheatfield with Crows
07 | Horizon -1 4.body:
A broad field opens beneath a deep blue sky. Three paths enter the wheat and divide the surface into directions that do not settle into a single route. Dark birds cross the sky. Their shapes are clear enough to attract attention and open enough to invite interpretation.

For many years, the painting has been described as Vincent's last work. The Van Gogh Museum cautions against that claim. Other paintings were made in Auvers after or around this moment, and the evidence does not provide a secure final sequence based on visual drama alone.

A late letter to Theo and Jo describes loneliness, sadness and the countryside's sustaining qualities in relation to a group of wheatfield paintings.  The words belong to the period. They do not turn the birds into a coded message or prove that the scene records a planned farewell.

This painting carries a large afterlife of interpretation. The exhibition places those interpretations beside the record of what can be established. Visitors can look at the branching paths and the moving birds while keeping the historical claim at the correct level of certainty.
07 | Horizon -1 4.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

07 | Horizon 1 0.title: Tree Roots
07 | Horizon 1 0.body:
The canvas is filled by trunks, roots, slope and patches of colour. The ground rises close to the viewer, leaving little distance for a horizon. The painting asks for a near view. Our eyes move through a tangled field of relationships, searching for the boundaries between root, earth and shadow.

The Van Gogh Museum describes the work as unfinished and probably Vincent's final painting.  That wording preserves a conclusion with a boundary around it. It records the museum's assessment while leaving room for chronology to remain a research question.

In 2020, Wouter van der Veen proposed a location in Auvers by comparing the painting with a historical postcard. Later historical photographs strengthened the place-based investigation.  The location helps us understand what kind of slope and trees Vincent may have been observing. It does not turn the painting into a map of the events that followed.

A later family letter by Andries Bonger describes a forest scene painted on the morning before Vincent's death. This testimony has influenced the work's afterlife, although it was written after the event and does not identify the canvas with complete certainty.

The image remains close to the ground. Its history moves between material evidence, place research and later memory. Each layer adds information. None should be allowed to close the painting too quickly.
07 | Horizon 1 0.collectionCredit: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

02 | North 01.title: Sorrow
02 | North 01.body:
The woman in this drawing is Clasina Maria Hoornik, known as Sien. When Vincent met her in The Hague, she was pregnant and caring for a young daughter. In a letter to Theo, he described sharing his limited resources with them and working with her as a model throughout the winter. Posing was difficult for Sien, and Vincent acknowledged how much her work had helped him learn.

Her head rests on her arms. A firm line follows the curve of her back. Vincent was exploring how an outline could carry feeling, drawing on his admiration for Millet. He returned to the subject in several versions.

In July, he described Sorrow as a small beginning in his ambition to make drawings that could move people.
02 | North 01.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; source file credits Christie's · Private collection · F929 / JH129
02 | North 01.provenanceNote: Identity follows the scholarly Van Gogh Letters edition. Collection names are documented source attributions, not independently verified current ownership.

02 | North 02.title: The Potato Eaters (oil painting)
02 | North 02.creator: Vincent van Gogh
02 | North 02.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
02 | North 02.body:
Five people gather around food and drink beneath a hanging lamp. Their faces and hands carry much of the painting’s weight.

Van Gogh had spent the winter studying heads and hands before attempting this demanding group composition. On 30 April 1885, he told Theo that the painting was still unfinished. He wanted viewers to connect the hands reaching towards the potatoes with the work of cultivating the earth.

The scene presents his understanding of rural labour and an earned meal. Its rough forms, closely considered colours, and concentrated light belong to a project in which he had invested months of work.
02 | North 02.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; original held by the Van Gogh Museum

04 | South 03.title: Sunflowers (Arles, London version)
04 | South 03.body:
In August 1888, Vincent was planning a studio decorated with sunflowers. Gauguin had yet to arrive in Arles. There were practical decisions to make about the pictures, their backgrounds and the space they would occupy. Vincent worked early, while the flowers were still fresh enough to paint.

Yellow spreads across this canvas through petals, vase and background. Small differences of texture and tone keep the forms distinct. The bouquet includes flowers opening, flowering and drying. These changes allow a reading of passing time, an interpretation developed by the National Gallery.

For this exhibition, the picture belongs to the activity of preparing a shared home. Its later fame can wait while we follow the work of making it.
04 | South 03.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; The National Gallery, London, NG3863

04 | South 04.title: Starry Night over the Rhône
04 | South 04.body: The Rhône at night, with lamplight reflected in the water. Not the later Starry Night of Saint-Rémy.
04 | South 04.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; original held by the Musée d'Orsay

05 | South 06.title: The Red Vineyard
05 | South 06.body:
Workers bend across a vineyard coloured red, orange and gold. The painting belongs to November 1888, during the period when Vincent and Gauguin were working in Arles. Later technical examination found changes beneath the visible surface, including a figure altered in the course of painting.

Its history extends to Brussels. In 1890, the painter Anna Boch purchased it at the exhibition of Les Vingt. The scholarly edition of Vincent's letters cites Theo's account book recording a receipt of 400 francs.

The picture connects labour in the fields with the labour of an artist seeking buyers. Its documented sale gives us a particular transaction, with a buyer, an exhibition and an account.
05 | South 06.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; source file names the Pushkin Museum
05 | South 06.institution: The Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow

06 | Curved wall 1 3.title: Almond Blossom
06 | Curved wall 1 3.body:
A new child entered the family while Vincent was in Saint-Rémy. Theo and Jo named their son Vincent Willem.

On 19 February 1890, Vincent wrote to his mother that he had begun a painting for the baby: large branches of white almond blossom against blue, intended for Theo and Jo's bedroom.

The branches spread across the canvas with little indication of the ground below. Flowers, buds and the spaces between them make the sky part of the design.

By June, Vincent reported that the picture hung above the piano in the family's apartment.  The work had a destination in an ordinary room. In this exhibition, that placement brings its later fame back to a particular relationship: an uncle making something for a child and the people who would raise him.
06 | Curved wall 1 3.credit: Image: Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; original held by the Van Gogh Museum
06 | Curved wall 1 3.institution: Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)
06 | Curved wall 1 3.storyGroup: A New Member of the Family

06 | Curved wall 1 4.title: Irises (garden)
06 | Curved wall 1 4.body:
During his first week at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole, Vincent began painting irises in the hospital garden. He considered the canvas a study.  A letter of 9 May mentions violet irises among the work already under way.

The flowers are close to us. Leaves cross one another, petals turn in different directions, and the composition continues beyond its edges. The space offers enough variation to keep looking.

The colours have a history of their own. Getty's conservation research shows that the flowers' present blue appearance was altered by the fading of red pigment in an original violet mixture.

Here, the garden enters the story through attention and material evidence. We see the image Vincent worked on, and we learn that even a familiar painting has changed during the time it has survived.
06 | Curved wall 1 4.credit: Image: Getty Open Content, via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain; Getty collection 826
06 | Curved wall 1 4.institution: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles
